title: San Francisco’s rank among peers, year by year
question: Has San Francisco’s position against comparable cities and city-plus-county pairs changed since 2015?
finding: San Francisco’s general public-service spending per resident went from $6,005 in fiscal 2017 to $10,517 in 2025 (75% more); the middle city-plus-county pair went from $3,207 to $5,855 (83% more). It ranked first against the pairs in every year. In fiscal 2024 its unfunded pension promise came to $4,668 per resident (rank 4 of 7; pair middle $4,187) and its retiree-health promise to $4,641 (rank 1; pair middle $1,572). Debt owed by its general funds was $5,465 per resident in fiscal 2025 (rank 1; pair middle $1,125).
how: San Francisco is a city and a county in one government. Every other city here sits inside a county that separately runs welfare, public health, jails and support for the courts for its residents, so setting San Francisco beside a city alone overstates the gap. The fairer comparison adds each city’s spending per city resident to its county’s spending per county resident. One row per fiscal year. Spending is the general public-service total of the previous screen and starts in 2017, when the State Controller’s city form began to separate self-supporting businesses. Taxes go back to 2015. Pension and retiree-health figures are the net amounts owed (promises less money set aside) in the State Controller’s tables, for the government’s own funds including its businesses. Debt is the principal still owed at year end on each bond and loan the report lists against general funds. Each rank counts San Francisco with the other cities alone, and with the city-plus-county pairs; 1 is the highest per resident. A blank means the State Controller’s files have no figure for that year for at least one place.
limits: Ranks among seven or eight places move on small differences. Pension figures jump with the stock market: San Francisco’s row for fiscal 2022 shows a pension surplus, after its pension fund earned 35.4% in the year to June 2021; a negative figure in that year is that surplus. Pension and retiree-health promises include workers in city-run businesses, which differ from place to place. Debt paid from the revenue of the airport, water, power, port and similar businesses is left out of the debt column. The State Controller’s retiree-health table for counties repeats the pension table to the dollar for fiscal 2018 (5 of the 5 counties used here), which looks like a publishing error in the source; those cells are left out, so no pair figure is given for retiree health in that year.
